scenes.headline: How a browser video editor draws one frame
scenes.sub: Integer time, the browser's decoder, a Rust GPU compositor.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Clip! Here's how a free browser video editor turns a timeline into frames, inside one tab.

scenes.text: Keep time as whole ticks, ask each clip which source frame it needs, decode with the browser, and composite the layers on the GPU.
scenes.say: The idea: keep time as whole ticks, ask each clip for one source frame, decode it with the browser, and stack the layers on the graphics card.

scenes.title: One frame, from timeline to file

steps.say: Every time is a whole number of ticks, a hundred and twenty thousand a second. For each frame, the resolver visits every clip.
A clip that covers this moment asks the browser's decoder for one source frame.
A Rust compositor, compiled for the web, stacks the layers on the graphics card, main track first.

steps.note: export repeats this once per frame
steps.say: Export runs that loop once per frame and keeps the whole file in memory.

scenes.title: Which source frame?
scenes.say: The arithmetic fits on one line.

parts.note: the playhead minus where the clip starts
parts.say: Clip time is the playhead minus where the clip starts.

parts.note: what was cut from the head of the source
parts.say: Add what was trimmed off the head.
Then scale by the clip's speed.

scenes.label: one frame at 29.97, an exact whole number
scenes.note: a float can't hold 1001/30000 of a second
scenes.say: Why ticks? At the broadcast rate, one frame is exactly four thousand and four ticks. In floating point seconds it never lands exactly.
